question.en: What is XSS, and how would you prevent it in a web application?

answer.en: XSS happens when untrusted input is interpreted as executable browser code. The defense depends on the output context: encode untrusted values for HTML, attribute, URL, or JavaScript contexts rather than relying on a blacklist. If users must author HTML, sanitize it with a well-maintained sanitizer. Use framework escaping by default and treat raw-HTML escape hatches as security-sensitive. CSP is a useful additional layer, but OWASP does not recommend it as the primary XSS defense. Also review client-side DOM sinks, because server-side filtering alone does not cover DOM-based XSS.

question.en: Your template HTML-encodes every user value, so `<` becomes `<`. A value still ends up inside `<a href="{{url}}">` and an attacker submits `javascript:alert(1)`. Why did encoding not help?

answer.en: HTML entity encoding protects markup structure, but in the href the value is interpreted as a URL, and `javascript:` is valid URL syntax, so the browser executes it on click. The value needs URL-context handling: validate or allowlist the scheme (http, https, or relative paths) and encode for the URL context, not just entity-encode for HTML.

question.en: All user input passes through a server-side HTML sanitizer before storage. Is the app now immune to XSS?

answer.en: No. Stored and reflected XSS through server output are covered, but DOM-based XSS happens in the browser: client-side script reads a source like location.hash or postMessage and writes it into a sink such as innerHTML. That data never crossed your server sanitizer. You must review client-side DOM sinks separately and keep framework escaping on for rendered output.

question.en: Why does CSRF occur, and what is a practical defense for cookie-authenticated requests?

answer.en: CSRF abuses the browser's automatic inclusion of authentication cookies: a malicious site induces the browser to send a state-changing request to the target site. Protect every state-changing endpoint with a server-validated CSRF token, preferably using framework support. A synchronizer token or a suitable double-submit design makes the request carry a value the attacker cannot read. SameSite cookies and Origin or Fetch Metadata checks can add defense in depth, but do not treat POST alone as protection. XSS can defeat CSRF controls, so prevent XSS separately. Keep state-changing operations out of GET.

question.en: We set SameSite=Lax on the session cookie. Is that enough to retire our CSRF tokens?

answer.en: No. Lax still sends the cookie on top-level cross-site GET navigations, so any state change reachable via GET stays exposed. SameSite and Origin or Fetch Metadata checks are defense in depth: every state-changing endpoint still needs a server-validated CSRF token, and state-changing operations must stay out of GET.

question.en: Every mutating endpoint validates a synchronizer token. A pentest still reports that one stored XSS gives them full account takeover. How, if CSRF was 'solved'?

answer.en: Because XSS is a strictly stronger attack. Script running on your origin operates inside the victim's session: it can read the token from the page or from any cookie the page can access, then issue same-origin requests that carry both the session cookie and a valid token. CSRF defenses assume the attacker cannot run script on your origin, so preventing XSS is a prerequisite, not an alternative.

question.en: What is the same-origin policy, and what does CORS actually change?

answer.en: An origin is the combination of scheme, host, and port. The same-origin policy restricts how a document or script from one origin can interact with another. CORS is an HTTP-header mechanism that lets a server declare which other origins a browser may read through APIs such as fetch. For non-simple requests, the browser may preflight with OPTIONS. CORS is not an authentication mechanism and does not make an endpoint private: it controls browser read access. For credentialed requests, the server must name an explicit allowed origin and allow credentials; `*` cannot be combined with credentials. The server must still authorize every request.

question.en: The API returns no CORS headers at all. Did the browser stop the evil site's request from reaching the server?

answer.en: Not necessarily. For requests that do not trigger a preflight (form posts, images, simple fetch calls) the request is still sent and the server still processes it; the same-origin policy and CORS stop the evil page's JavaScript from reading the response. That is why state-changing endpoints need CSRF defenses and server-side authorization regardless of CORS.

question.en: We never configured CORS, so our API is private and only our frontend can use it, right?

answer.en: No. CORS only controls which origins a browser will let script read responses from. It is not an authentication mechanism and does not make an endpoint private: curl, a server-side client, or any non-browser tool ignores it entirely. The server must authenticate and authorize every request independently of CORS.

question.en: How would you design a CSP for an application, and what makes a policy strict?
Why is a nonce-based `script-src` considered stricter than allowlisting script hosts like `https://cdn.example.com`?

answer.en: A nonce policy is tied to the exact scripts intentionally emitted in that specific response: any other inline or injected script without the nonce is blocked. A host allowlist trusts every script that host will ever serve, so a single bypass on that host (an uploaded file, a JSONP-style endpoint, an open redirect serving script) unlocks execution for the whole policy, and broad allowlists are easy to misconfigure.

question.en: A review finds that the CSP nonce is generated once at deploy time and reused on every response for a week. Is that still a strict policy?

answer.en: No. The nonce must be unpredictable and match only the scripts intentionally emitted in that response. If it is static or predictable, any injection that can learn the nonce from a cached page, a log, or a previous response can simply carry it and execute. Generate a fresh high-entropy nonce per response and emit it only in the CSP header and the intended script tags.

question.en: How would you review a credentialed CORS design for a multi-tenant API?

answer.en: Start with an explicit inventory of browser clients and the resources each must read; do not enable CORS globally by default. Compare the request Origin against a controlled, tenant-aware allowlist and return one exact allowed origin, never an arbitrary reflection. Add `Vary: Origin` when responses differ by Origin. For credentialed requests, set `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` only where required and never combine it with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. Validate preflight methods and headers, but remember that CORS is a browser read policy, not authorization. The API must enforce tenant authorization independently, and cookie SameSite policy and CSRF defenses must be reviewed together.

question.en: The API gateway checks the Origin against `*.partner.acme.test` and echoes the request Origin back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin when it matches. Why is this flagged in review?

answer.en: Two issues. First, the response must be one exact origin from a controlled, tenant-aware allowlist, never an arbitrary reflection; echoing whatever matched a pattern admits any origin satisfying it, including hosts a tenant stood up without review. Second, wildcard subdomain trust is not tenant-aware: any host under that suffix, including a compromised or attacker-registered subdomain, becomes a credentialed reader of the API.

question.en: Responses include Access-Control-Allow-Origin only for allowlisted origins, but the CDN in front of the API caches them without any Origin awareness. What breaks?

answer.en: Cache poisoning of the CORS headers. The CDN can cache a response negotiated for one origin (with that origin's ACAO and credentials flag) and serve it to a different origin's request, either breaking legitimate clients or handing a disallowed origin a cached response that appears to permit its read. Any response that varies by Origin must carry `Vary: Origin` so intermediaries key their cache on it.

question.en: What controls would you put around third-party dependencies and the software supply chain?

answer.en: Maintain an inventory or SBOM covering direct and transitive dependencies, and continuously monitor reliable vulnerability sources. Use lockfiles and reviewed, intentionally selected versions rather than resolving whatever is newest at build time. Route package retrieval through a controlled proxy or internal registry where feasible, verify checksums or signatures, and protect private package scopes against dependency confusion. Review install scripts and isolate builds so untrusted package code cannot read CI secrets. Secure source control and CI with least privilege, protected branches, MFA, auditable changes, and signed or provenance-backed artifacts. Patch according to exploitability and exposure, not only a scanner's severity number.

question.en: The repo pins every dependency with a lockfile and CI installs with a frozen lockfile. Why does the supply-chain review still find gaps?

answer.en: Pinning prevents drift, not compromise. The pinned versions can still get a new advisory tomorrow; install scripts still execute untrusted package code in CI where secrets live; a private scope that is not protected can be resolved from a public registry (dependency confusion); and artifacts can be tampered with if nothing verifies checksums or signatures. The control set is lockfiles plus a controlled proxy or internal registry, integrity verification, install-script review, isolated builds, and continuous monitoring of vulnerability sources.

question.en: Your package `@acme/ui` exists only in your internal registry. Where does dependency confusion come from, and what stops it?

answer.en: It comes from resolvers that fall back to public registries: if a build or a developer machine resolves `@acme/ui` from a public registry, an attacker who published that exact name there feeds you their code. The defenses are to protect the private package scope (registry-side reservation and access control), route package retrieval through a controlled proxy or internal registry that does not silently fall back, and verify checksums or signatures so substituted artifacts fail.

question.en: A scanner reports a vulnerability in a transitive dependency. How do you decide what to do?

answer.en: First identify the affected version, the dependency path, the vulnerable code path, and whether the deployed product is reachable and exploitable. Confirm the advisory using a trusted vulnerability source and assess exposure, compensating controls, and business impact rather than blindly applying a score. Prefer upgrading the direct dependency to pull a fixed transitive version; if that is impossible, apply a vendor patch, replace the component, or add a narrowly scoped mitigation while tracking an owner and deadline. Test the fix with regression or exploit-focused coverage. Document accepted risk with an accountable approver and keep monitoring until the vulnerable component is removed or patched.

question.en: A scanner files a ticket: CVSS 9.8 in a transitive dependency your service pulls in. The vulnerable code path is a parser your service never invokes. Do you page the on-call and deploy tonight?

answer.en: No, you investigate first. Identify the affected version and dependency path, confirm the advisory with a trusted vulnerability source, and determine whether the deployed product is reachable and exploitable: an unreachable code path with compensating controls is a different risk than an exposed one. Patching follows exploitability and exposure, not the scanner's severity number; the finding still gets an owner, a deadline, and a documented decision.

question.en: The advisory affects version 2.x, your app pins 2.3.1, and no fixed release exists yet. What are your options besides waiting?

answer.en: Work the alternatives in order of preference: upgrade the direct dependency if any version pulls a fixed transitive one; apply a vendor patch if one ships outside the mainline; replace the component; or add a narrowly scoped mitigation (blocking the vulnerable entry point, a WAF rule, disabling the affected feature) while tracking an owner and a deadline. If risk is accepted, document it with an accountable approver and keep monitoring until the component is patched or removed.
